etymologies.etymologyHTML: 1655, from French gril, from Middle French gril, from Old French greïl, graïl (“gridiron”), from graïlle (“grate, grating”), from Latin crātīcula (“gridiron”), diminutive of crātis (“hurdle, wickerwork”), q.v. Related to griddle, hurdle.

definitions.definition: A grating; a grid of wire or a sheet of material with a pattern of holes or slots, usually used to protect something while allowing the passage of air and liquids. Typical uses: to allow air through a fan while preventing fingers or objects from passing; to allow people to talk to somebody, while preventing attack.
The criss-cross pieces that separate panes of glass in a window.

quote.citation: 1907 August, Robert W[illiam] Chambers, chapter I, in The Younger Set, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: The house was a big elaborate limestone affair, evidently new. Winter sunshine sparkled on lace-hung casement, on glass marquise, and the burnished bronze foliations of grille and door.

definitions.definition: On a vehicle, a slotted cover as above, to protect and hide the radiator, while admitting air to cool it.
(UK) A cooking device comprising a source of radiative heat and a means of holding food under it; a broiler in US English
(US) A cooking device comprising a source of radiative and convective heat and a means of holding food above it; a barbecue.
Food (designed to be) cooked on a grill.
A grillroom; a restaurant serving grilled food.

quote.text: Everyone's meeting at the new grill in town! And everyone's having a real good time! They're drinking frozen blue Margaritas. Munching on Cajun popcorn shrimp. Laughing with old friends and getting to know new ones.

definitions.definition: (colloquial) A type of jewelry worn on the front teeth.

quote.citation: 2021, Zakiya Dalila Harris, The Other Black Girl, Bloomsbury, page 213:
quote.text: Nella wished him luck and started to walk away, still unsure if that glint in his mouth was a grill or just a few golden teeth.

definitions.definition: (colloquial, by extension) The front teeth regarded collectively.
(Internet slang, humorous) Deliberate misspelling of girl.
(transitive) To cook (food) on a grill; to barbecue.
(transitive, Australia, New Zealand, UK) To cook food under the element of a stove or only under the top element of an oven – (US) broil, (cooking) salamander.

quote.citation: 1938, Norman Lindsay, Age of Consent, 1st Australian edition, Sydney, N.S.W.: Ure Smith, published 1962, →OCLC, page 139:
quote.text: Bradly hung the fowl in a sugar-bag for to-morrow's dinner and set about grilling chops, with tomatoes stuffed with cheese and breadcrumbs in the pan.

definitions.definition: (transitive, colloquial) To interrogate; to question aggressively or harshly.

quote.citation: 2006, Noire [pseudonym], Thug-A-Licious: An Urban Erotic Tale, New York, N.Y.: One World, Ballantine Books, →ISBN, page 148:
quote.text: The white cop grilled me. He was tall, but had a stomach like a pregnant woman. The other two were brothers, and they looked like they just didn't wanna be standing there.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, informal) To feel very hot; to swelter.

quote.text: He had grilled in the heat, sweated in the rains, and shivered with fever under the rude thatch roof;  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To stamp or mark with a grill.
(New York City) To stare at.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English grillen (“to anger, provoke”), from Old English grillan, griellan (“to annoy, vex, offend”), from Proto-West Germanic *gralljan (“to shout, make angry”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian grulje (“to make angry”), Dutch grillen (“to shudder, shiver”), Low German vergrellen (“to anger, provoke”), German grollen (“to rumble”) and perhaps also with French grouiller (“to swarm”).

definitions.definition: (transitive, Scotland, US, obsolete) To make angry; provoke; offend, incite.
(transitive, chiefly Scotland, obsolete) To terrify; make tremble.
(intransitive, chiefly Scotland, obsolete) To tremble; shiver.
(intransitive, Northern England, Scotland, obsolete) To snarl; snap.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English gril, grille (“harsh, rough, severe”), from Old English *grielle, from Proto-West Germanic *grallī (“angry”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer- (“to rattle, make a noise, grumble”). Cognate with German grell (“harsh, angry”), Danish grel (“shrill, glaring, dazzling”).

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Harsh, rough, severe; cruel.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English grille, from Old English *grylla, *griella, from Proto-West Germanic *gralljō.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Harm.
